cover.title: Put a behaviour policy on your agent, in five minutes.

items.html:
Ask your assistant to do something. Paste one line that says it must not. Ask again, and watch it refuse. That line is the first row of an Agent Behaviour Policy, and it takes five minutes to see, in Claude or ChatGPT, in your browser, with nothing to install.

customers.riskmandate.ai: six examples, simplest first.

Three steps

  1. Ask. "Say hello to me." The assistant does it.
  2. Add the line. "Behaviour policy for this chat: you must never write the word hello, in any language." Ask again; it refuses, and says why.
  3. New chat. The line first, then the question. It refuses from the start.

Watch for the loophole: some replies say "Hi!" instead. The line named a word, not a greeting. Most of the work of a behaviour policy is saying what you mean.

From hello world to refunds

The six examples go one step at a time: stay on topic, no web search, keep a secret, drafts and not sends, and refunds. The last one is the business case in a single exchange: the assistant could refund £180 all along, and what stood between the customer and the money was what it was told.

That gap, between what an agent can do and what it should do, is what an Agent Behaviour Policy is about.

What the line is, and what it is not

In every example the assistant keeps the line because it chooses to. That is an expectation, the weakest of four barriers: none, an expectation, a setting, a boundary. Only a boundary, a rule kept by something the agent cannot reach, is a control in the strict sense. The examples are where the idea starts, not where it ends.

The full ABP writes down, for one agent in one deployment, everything it can reach, what you authorised it to do, the gap between the two, and what stands in the way of each thing. It describes and does not judge, so it carries no score.

Try it, and tell us

Every example ends with five questions, and the answers come to us encrypted in your browser. Start with hello world: customers.riskmandate.ai.

items.html:
Most AI agents can do far more than anyone authorised, and nobody has written down the difference. An Agent Behaviour Policy is that record: for one agent in one deployment, everything it can reach, what you authorised it to do, the gap between the two, and what actually stands in the way of each thing.

Four words

  • Grant: what the agent can reach, read from the deployment, not from the brochure.
  • Mandate: what the business authorised it to do, and why.
  • Gap: the difference. "Your agent can do three hundred and forty things and you authorised twelve" is a finding.
  • Barrier: for each thing in the gap, what stands in the way: nothing, an expectation, a setting, or a boundary.

The gate in the middle is yours: your gateway, proxy or identity provider, configured from the rules in the ABP.

Not in the request path, on purpose

RiskMandate is read-only. Enforcing belongs to the gateways, hooks and runtimes you already run; the ABP is what they enforce, and it says which of them holds each rule, or that nothing does. It carries no score and no verdict. It is the record.

Only a rule kept out of the agent's reach is a control.

Which agents

Commercial ones, today: Claude with Gmail or Microsoft 365, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Google Workspace connectors, GitHub Actions. Sixteen example policies are published, free, each from the vendor's own pages, quoted and dated.

How it gets into the room

Through the questions that already arrive: a customer's security questionnaire, a contract clause, an insurance renewal, a board asking what the agents can do. Or twenty minutes with one agent that worries you.

The quickest start is five minutes in your own assistant: customers.riskmandate.ai. The full argument is on the newsroom: What can your agent reach?

items.title: A prompt asks. A boundary enforces.
items.why: The idea people remember: how much of an agent's safety is hope. Three newsroom pieces in one.

cover.kicker: Hope, a check, or a control
cover.title: A prompt asks. A boundary enforces.

items.html:
Every rule an agent follows is kept by something. The question that matters is what.

Three levels

  • Told: a sentence in the prompt, kept by the model. An expectation: hope.
  • Checked: a hook in the agent's harness that inspects each action. Deterministic, but on the agent's own machine.
  • Never given: the agent asks, and something out of its reach holds the key. A boundary: a control.

One agent, three designs

The newsroom built one customer-service agent three ways and gave each an ABP, every rule marked by what enforces it. The same 62 fictional emails, sixteen of them hostile, went through all three. In the first design 97% of the rules were hope; in the second 73%; in the third 23%.

A key can leak through an allowed action

Sending an email is a capability; putting an API key in it is content. A policy that covers secrets needs rows about content too, each with its barrier. A hook tested against nine ways a secret tries to leave caught most of them and missed three: a key in base64, a key split in two, and a file piped straight out. That is why the strongest level is the one where the key is never given.

A rule the agent can rewrite is a setting, not a control.

An ABP does not enforce anything itself. It governs: it says what each agent is granted and for, writes each rule down, and names the level that keeps it, so you can see how much is hope.

Try the told level yourself, and watch where it holds and where it bends: keep a secret, on customers.riskmandate.ai.

Ten hard questions, the ones people actually ask about a product like ours:

What happens when an agent bypasses its policy? Who enforces? Who is liable when it goes wrong? What stops a big platform absorbing you? What about agents instructing agents? What can you measure?

My co-founder brought them back from a conference. We answered them in a two-hour interview, with an honest table of what is live and what is still design, and a list of what we are deliberately not: not inline, not an insurer, not a one-button solution.

Agent Behaviour Policies are ready for the next level. What is left is execution, and execution starts with customers.

So the first batch are customers, not beta users. Each starts with credit to spend on a site we run, follows six examples, and is followed up closely by us, with objectives and milestones written with them.

What we want to find

The usage moment. The simplest useful policy, the easiest entry, a fair price.

Seven milestones run from "in, with credit" to that moment. The site publishes them, with every review of it and what we did about each one.

How the site works

  • £50 of credit for reading, not money. Each page draws a few pence from it; nothing is billed and nothing is blocked.
  • Feedback encrypted in your browser, to a key only RiskMandate holds, under every example.
  • Six installable policies for Claude Code, ChatGPT and Claude, from one line to a line and a hook.

The next batch

The next batch is open. Start with the examples at customers.riskmandate.ai, and to join, email agent@riskmandate.ai with the subject "Next batch".

items.title: Post: free to copy, paid at the source
items.why: Why the policies are open and still a business. A short idea that invites argument.
items.text:
Our behaviour policies and hooks are open, CC BY 4.0 and Apache 2.0. Anyone may copy them.

But a hook is code. It runs on your machine, with your permissions. A company will not take one from a site it does not know, any more than it would install software from one.

So the official source, with its reviews and its signatures, is where people will come, even for something free to copy, and it can charge per use there. To earn that, it cannot be us saying "trust us": the hooks above all should be reviewed and audited by others, and signed.

The argument: https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/free-to-copy-paid-at-the-source.html

cover.title: From one policy to agents an insurer can cover.

items.html:
RiskMandate's founders are discussing a roadmap, and it reads as a spectrum of trust: each stage answers the next question a customer asks once the last one is answered. It is a proposal, not a decision, and we are on the first stage.

Six stages

  1. Policies. What each agent can reach, what it may do, the gap. We can create them today.
  2. Understand. Where are our agents, what can they reach, what is our exposure?
  3. Risk acceptance. Which of these risks do we carry, and who decides?
  4. Contain. Make the blast radius smaller.
  5. Manage. Run the agents as a fleet.
  6. Insure. By then the evidence an insurer needs exists.
Then insure. The end game: agents an insurer can cover.

RiskMandate is not an insurer. Its aim is to make agentic AI insurable, and the site already shows the next two documents: a Licence to Operate for a whole deployment, and the Insurability Index, in design.

The description should not belong to the seller

A description of what an agent can do should not belong to the company that sells it. So the ABP vocabulary is open, and on 20 October we proposed that it become the first hosted project of the Open Security Summit, a UK community interest company, with a public charter and a steering group with a majority independent of RiskMandate still to be written. Hosting is not independence; the charter is what will make it so.

Every stage starts with the first one, and the first one takes five minutes: customers.riskmandate.ai.
